# The steeper 1/f slope of MEG power spectrum is associated with stronger gamma synchrony, measured via inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) in the 40-Hz auditory steady-state response

## Introduction

Coordinated activity of neurons and robust mechanisms to respond to external stimuli are crucial for brain function and its role in organism survival. Neural phase-locking represents a fundamental process where local neuronal ensembles synchronize their oscillatory activity to external rhythmic stimuli, enabling precise temporal coordination of neural responses. Among the various frequency bands of neural oscillations, gamma-band activity (30-100 Hz) serves as a particularly important mechanism for local circuit coordination and stimulus-locked information processing [@fries2009NeuronalGammaBandSynchronization]. However, traditional approaches to studying neural phase-locking often examine oscillatory activity in isolation, without considering how it relates to other neural markers that may reflect similar underlying physiological mechanisms.

Understanding the relationship between different electrophysiological measures is becoming increasingly important as researchers seek biomarkers for brain health and its dysfunctions. Among the measures that have emerged as potentially important indices of brain activity [@pellegrino2024AssessingCorticalExcitability] are gamma-band synchrony (estimated via the ability of neural populations to maintain consistent phase relationships to external stimuli across repeated presentations) and the 1/f component of neural power spectra (spectral slope). Both may reflect fundamental properties of local neural circuits, particularly the balance between excitation and inhibition (E/I balance), yet they are rarely examined together within the same experimental framework.

### Neural oscillations and gamma synchrony

Neuronal oscillations are rhythmic changes in neuronal ensembles between high and low excitability states [@schroeder2009LowfrequencyNeuronalOscillations]. They shape sensory, motor and cognitive processes [@henao2020EntrainmentSynchronizationBrain] and are thought to be the building blocks of fast-scale information processing in the brain, serving as a mechanism for synchronizing neural activity across distributed regions [@womelsdorf2007ModulationNeuronalInteractions]. During oscillations, the probability of neuron discharge is modulated by local extracellular and membrane potentials that in turn are reflected by the phase [@henao2020EntrainmentSynchronizationBrain]. This might create a "window of integration," where stimuli falling within the high excitability part of the cycle might be integrated, especially through gamma oscillation [@fries2009NeuronalGammaBandSynchronization].

Gamma oscillations occupy a unique position in this oscillatory hierarchy due to their role in local circuit dynamics and stimulus processing. They are primarily generated by parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons through precisely timed interactions with pyramidal neurons [@bartos2007SynapticMechanismsSynchronized]. As @fries2009NeuronalGammaBandSynchronization and @fries2015RhythmsCognitionCommunication argue, gamma-band activity enables cortical computation through precise temporal coordination that allows for both selectivity and invariance of neuronal responses. This coordination enables functional segmentation of neural processing, where local populations can phase-lock to relevant stimuli while maintaining independence from irrelevant inputs.

The capacity for gamma synchrony—the ability of neural populations to consistently align their oscillatory activity to external rhythmic stimuli across multiple stimulus presentations [@schuler2022AuditoryDrivenGamma]—is critical for normal brain function. Alterations in this phase-locking capacity often indicate pathological conditions [@pellegrino2019CorticalGammasynchronyMeasured]. Changes in local gamma phase-locking have been consistently observed in various neuropsychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorders, and bipolar disorder, making it an important biomarker for local circuit dysfunction [@parciauskaite2021GammaRangeAuditorySteadyState].

### Auditory Steady-State Responses (ASSR) as a tool for studying neural synchrony

The auditory steady-state response (ASSR) represents the ability of neural populations to phase-lock their oscillatory activity to the frequency and phase of repetitive auditory stimuli and provides a robust experimental paradigm for investigating local gamma synchrony in controlled laboratory conditions. @lakatos2019NewUnifyingAccount defined entrainment as phase locking resulting from (predominantly) unidirectional coupling.

The 40-Hz ASSR has emerged as a particularly valuable tool for studying local gamma phase-locking. @tada2020GammaBandAuditorySteadyState indicate that the 40-Hz ASSR is generated primarily through synaptic interactions between parvalbumin-positive GABAergic interneurons and pyramidal neurons, making it a direct probe of the local neural circuits that regulate E/I balance. This response is primarily generated in the medial region of the primary auditory cortex, with additional contributions from thalamic and corticothalamic sources, and recent evidence suggests significant involvement of prefrontal cortex in gamma-range ASSR generation [@parciauskaite2021GammaRangeAuditorySteadyState].

The 40-Hz ASSR shows several characteristics that make it particularly useful for research into local phase-locking mechanisms. It demonstrates high test-retest reliability and can be measured consistently across different species, facilitating translational research [@tan2015MEGmeasuredAuditorySteadystate]. The response can be elicited reliably across various populations, though it shows both inter- and intra-subject variability that may reflect meaningful individual differences in local neural circuit properties. Importantly, ASSR phase-locking deficits have been documented as early indicators of brain dysfunction, appearing in at-risk populations before the onset of clinical symptoms [@tada2020GammaBandAuditorySteadyState].

Research by @parciauskaite2021GammaRangeAuditorySteadyState demonstrates that gamma-range ASSR phase-locking ability is related to cognitive flexibility and reasoning abilities in healthy participants, and to memory and processing speed in patients with schizophrenia. These findings suggest that individual differences in gamma-range ASSR reflect important aspects of local circuit functioning, including the precision of stimulus-locked neural responses and the stability of local gamma-generating networks.

### Aperiodic neural activity and the 1/f slope

Complementary to rhythmic neural activity, electrophysiological signals contain a prominent component that follows a 1/f power law. This component has a characteristic shape where power decreases exponentially with increasing frequency, creating a linear relationship when plotted in log-log space [@donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower]. The 1/f component (slope) can be characterized by two main parameters: an offset that reflects broadband power across all frequencies, and an exponent (slope) that determines the rate of power decay across frequencies.

Traditionally, this aperiodic activity was considered neural "noise" and was either ignored or statistically removed from analyses. However, mounting evidence demonstrates that the aperiodic component contains meaningful physiological information [@donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower]. Neuronal spiking is positively correlated with broadband LFP power [@manning2009BroadbandShiftsLocal]. The aperiodic offset correlates with neuronal population spiking activity and the BOLD signal from functional MRI, suggesting it reflects the overall level of neural activity. More intriguingly, the aperiodic exponent has been linked to the integration of underlying synaptic currents, which have stereotyped temporal dynamics that naturally give rise to the 1/f-like nature of neural power spectra.

@gao2017InferringSynapticExcitation propose that the aperiodic exponent reflects the balance between excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents. Excitatory currents, particularly those mediated by AMPA receptors, have relatively fast time constants and contribute to flatter power spectra (lower exponents). In contrast, inhibitory GABA currents have slower time constants and contribute to steeper power spectra (higher exponents). This means that the exponent will be lower when excitation dominates and higher when inhibition is stronger, providing a potential non-invasive marker of E/I balance.

The clinical and developmental relevance of the aperiodic exponent is becoming increasingly apparent. Changes in spectral slope have been documented across the lifespan, with systematic alterations observed in aging [@voytek2015AgeRelatedChangesNeural] and various neuropsychiatric conditions. The slope shows trait-like properties that are stable within individuals but vary meaningfully between individuals and groups, suggesting it may serve as a biomarker for brain function and dysfunction [@ahmad2022MechanismsMarkersNovel].

### Potential relationships between 1/f slope and gamma phase-locking

The relationship between the aperiodic exponent and local gamma synchrony could arise through multiple, non-mutually exclusive mechanisms. The most straightforward connection is biological: both measures may reflect shared underlying processes related to local E/I balance. If gamma synchrony depends on the precise timing and strength of inhibitory interneuron function, and the aperiodic exponent reflects the relative strength of excitatory versus inhibitory currents within local circuits, then systematic relationships between these measures would be expected across individuals and brain regions.

Supporting this biological connection, both ASSR phase-locking deficits and changes in aperiodic slope co-occur in similar neuropsychiatric conditions. For example, schizophrenia is characterized by both reduced 40-Hz ASSR phase-locking and altered 1/f slopes [@martinez-canada2023CombiningAperiodicSlopes]. Similarly, autism spectrum disorders show both local gamma phase-locking deficits and changes in aperiodic activity. These parallel alterations suggest that both measures may be influenced by common pathophysiological mechanisms, particularly those involving GABAergic interneuron function and NMDA receptor-mediated excitation within local circuits.

However, the relationship between these measures may also have important methodological components. Recent work by @samaha2022PowerSpectrumSlope demonstrates that the slope of the power spectrum can systematically confound estimation of oscillatory properties, including instantaneous frequency and phase measurements. Since inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) depends critically on consistent phase relationships across trials within a given brain region, systematic variations in spectral slope could introduce bias in local phase-locking estimates that is independent of any true biological relationship.

This methodological concern is particularly relevant for ITPC measurements when signals lack clear oscillatory peaks above the aperiodic background, or when signal-to-noise ratios are low due to dominant 1/f components [@zrenner2020ShakyGroundTruth]. In such cases, the phase values obtained from standard time-frequency analysis methods may become unreliable, potentially leading to spurious correlations between 1/f slope and apparent changes in measures of synchrony [@vandiepen2018CaveatsObservingInterTrial]. The concept of "phase" is inherently linked to rhythmic oscillations, and when clear oscillatory activity is difficult to distinguish from 1/f background activity, phase-based measures like ITPC may be systematically biased by the spectral slope [@wodeyar2023DifferentMethodsEstimate].

### Current study

This study investigates the relationship between the aperiodic spectral exponent and local gamma phase-locking as measured by ITPC during 40-Hz ASSR in healthy participants. We analyzed MEG data from 15 participants during auditory stimulation.

Our analytical strategy utilizes Bayesian multilevel modeling implemented through the Region-Based Analysis (RBA) framework [@chen2019HandlingMultiplicityNeuroimaging] to examine how spectral slope might be related to ITPC measured across brain regions while appropriately handling the multiple comparisons inherent in whole-brain analysis. This approach allows us to take into account region-specific effects while borrowing strength across regions through partial pooling, providing more robust and interpretable results than traditional mass-univariate approaches.

Understanding the relationship between these two putative biomarkers of local neural circuit function has important implications for their use in clinical and research contexts. If they reflect shared biological mechanisms, their combined examination may provide more sensitive and specific markers of local circuit integrity than either measure alone.

::: {.callout-warning}
## To address
Definitive testing of the biological relationship is challenging. However, we can partially test the methodological confound hypothesis with simulations of signals with varying parameters. The slope-ITPC relationship may partially reflect methodological interdependencies in phase estimation, where steeper slopes (indicating stronger high-frequency attenuation) systematically bias ITPC measurements toward lower values by reducing the signal-to-noise ratio of oscillatory components relative to aperiodic background.
:::

## Methods

### Participants and experimental design

This study analyzed a magnetoencephalography (MEG) dataset previously described by @pellegrino2019TranscranialDirectCurrent. The experimental procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee of the Province of Venice, and all participants provided written informed consent before participation.

Fifteen healthy, right-handed volunteers participated (12 females, 3 males; mean age = 28.8 ± 3 years, age range: 20-50 years). Participants were screened using the following exclusion criteria: (1) hearing impairment, (2) current use of medications affecting the central nervous system, (3) history of neuropsychiatric disorders, and (4) any other medical condition that might affect brain function.

The experiment used a within-subjects design to investigate cortical gamma-band synchronization in response to 40 Hz amplitude-modulated auditory stimuli. As shown in @fig-factors, the protocol comprised two different sessions of bi-hemispheric tDCS stimulation (sham and real) conducted at least 20 hours apart, indicated by condition (T): REAL or SHAM. The order of the tDCS stimulation (sham and real) was counterbalanced across subjects. Stimulation was applied to the left and right pericentral regions (@fig-factors) using standard protocols. The anode was positioned over the left hemisphere and the cathode over the right hemisphere, targeting auditory cortical regions. Real stimulation lasted 20 min with 20 s of fade-in and fade-out. Sham stimulation was performed with the same settings, but electrical current was delivered only for 20 s at the beginning and at the end of the tDCS session.

![Design of the original experiment. Source: @pellegrino2019TranscranialDirectCurrent](figures/chapter4/ch04-1-factors.png){#fig-factors fig-scap='Experimental design'}

Each session included two blocks corresponding to conditions related to the time (P) of applying tDCS stimulation: PRE (before tDCS) and POST (after tDCS). @fig-sound2 shows the structure of a paradigm used to induce 40 Hz synchrony during a single block. Each block consisted of 180 repetitions lasting 2 s each. Each trial included 1 s of pause (S=PRESTIM condition) followed by a 40 Hz amplitude-modulated (AM) tone (S=STIM condition), so that the stimulus onset asynchrony was 2 s. Each block lasted a total of 6 minutes (180 trials × 2 seconds). @fig-sound1 illustrates the auditory stimulus, an amplitude modulated tone with the following parameters: carrier frequency = 1,000 Hz and amplitude modulating frequency = 40 Hz.

::: {#fig-signal layout-ncol=2}
![Structure of the trial](figures/chapter4/experimental_protocol_sound2.png){#fig-sound2}

![Carrier and amplitude modulation](figures/chapter4/experimental_protocol_sound1.png){#fig-sound1}

Structure of auditory stimulation. Adapted from @pellegrino2019TranscranialDirectCurrent.
:::

### MEG data acquisition and preprocessing

MEG scans were performed at the MEGLab of the IRCCS San Camillo Hospital in Venice in a shielded room with a CTF-MEG system equipped with 275 gradiometers. As outlined in @pellegrino2019TranscranialDirectCurrent, MEG data preprocessing included: third-order spatial gradient noise cancellation, downsampling to 600 Hz, and signal space-separation. Heartbeat and eye-movement artifacts were cleaned with the SSP approach. MEG data was cut in 3 s epochs ranging from −1.5 s to +1.5 s around the 40 Hz sound onset. Epochs were visually inspected and those affected by artifacts were manually rejected. 

The available MRI scans were segmented and processed through FreeSurfer software. The surface was divided into 15,000 vertices imported into Brainstorm toolbox and downsampled into 8,000 vertices. The coregistration between functional MEG data and anatomical MRI data was performed via the Brainstorm toolbox.

Data was bandpass filtered between 2 and 80 Hz and then notch filtered for 50 Hz. The inverse problem for source estimation was solved with the whitened and depth-weighted linear L2-minimum norm estimate, with the dipole orientation constrained to be normal to the cortical surface. A common imaging kernel was computed and then applied to obtain single epoch cortical reconstructions. Data was projected into regions using the @destrieux2010AutomaticParcellationHuman atlas and exported from Brainstorm into MNE Python.

### Power spectral density and aperiodic parameterization

For every trial, the 1 s fragment before sound stimulation and 1 s fragment during the sound stimulation was extracted. For those intervals, power spectral density was computed using MNE Python using the `welch` method and the median was taken across trials in a block (as this is more robust than averaging). Then the slope and exponent of the spectrum were computed for each region of interest using the `specparam` toolbox [@donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower].

In the algorithm, the power spectrum PSD is modeled as a combination of the aperiodic component AP and a sum of N oscillatory peaks modeled as Gaussians:

$$
P = AP + \sum_{n=0}^N G_n
$$

The component $AP(f)$ for frequency $f$ can be expressed by the formula:

$$
AP(f) = b - \log(k + f^\chi)
$$

where $b$ is the broadband offset, $\chi$ is the exponent and $k$ is the knee parameter. The exponent $\chi$ is related to the negative slope of the power spectrum in log-log space, that is, the inverse relationship between power and frequency. The offset $b$ describes the uniform shift in power across frequencies.

The frequency range on which the algorithm was fitted spans the interval [3, 45] Hz. The parameters with which data were analyzed are the following hyperparameters: `peak_width_limits` = [1, 8], `min_peak_height` = 0.15, `peak_threshold` = 2.0.

### Estimation of synchrony via inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC)

Spectral modulations and phase consistency of ASSR in MEG and EEG data are highly reproducible, providing support for research [@tan2015MEGmeasuredAuditorySteadystate; @pellegrino2019TranscranialDirectCurrent]. ASSR are usually investigated by looking at the inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC). The inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) is defined using the length of the mean phase angle:

$$
\text{ITPC} = \left| \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^{N} e^{i \cdot \phi_k} \right|
$$

where $N$ represents the number of trials, $e^{i\phi_k}$ is the complex polar representation of the phase angle $\phi$ of trial $k$. ITPC is a measure of phase consistency over trials and can take values between 0 and 1. The higher the ITPC, the higher the 40 Hz gamma synchronization.

The ITPC was computed for 1 s pre-stimulus period and 1 s stimulation period via Time-Frequency Representation (TFR) using Morlet wavelets approach implemented in MNE Python (version 1.9) in the 39-41 Hz gamma band for each epoch. Values of ITPC were extracted in the period of -500 ms to -200 ms before sound stimulation starts and 300 ms to 700 ms during the sound stimulation, accounting for the time for brain to reach steady-state [@pellegrino2019TranscranialDirectCurrent], and averaged in those periods.

### Statistical analysis

All statistical analyses were conducted using Bayesian multilevel modeling implemented via the Region-Based Analysis (RBA) program [@chen2019HandlingMultiplicityNeuroimaging] from the AFNI software suite. RBA employs Bayesian inference through the `brms` package [@burkner2017BrmsPackageBayesian] and Stan probabilistic programming language, but provides a neuroimaging-optimized interface for handling the complex nested structure of our data (regions nested within subjects, repeated measures within subjects).

#### Preliminary analyses of experimental conditions

Due to the high-dimensional nature of our data (148 regions × 15 subjects × 4 conditions) and computational constraints, we first conducted preliminary analyses to determine whether data could be pooled across tDCS conditions. 

**Testing tDCS effects on ITPC:** We fitted separate Bayesian multilevel models for ITPC to test whether tDCS intervention affected phase-locking:

$$
\text{ITPC} \sim 1 + P \times T + (1 + P \times T | \text{subject}) + (1 | \text{ROI})
$$

where $P$ represents time point (PRE vs. POST tDCS) and $T$ represents stimulation type (REAL vs. SHAM). We employed a Student's t-distribution likelihood (df = 3) to accommodate potential outliers. Models were fitted using 4 MCMC chains with 4,000 iterations each (1,000 warmup), with `adapt_delta` set to 0.95.

::: {.callout-note}
## Results of preliminary analysis
The preliminary analysis revealed no regions with strong evidence (P+ > 0.975 or < 0.025) for differences between PRE-REAL and PRE-SHAM conditions, or for tDCS effects (POST vs. PRE). This allowed us to pool data across tDCS conditions for subsequent analyses.
:::

**Testing effects on spectral parameters:** Similar models were fitted to test whether tDCS or auditory stimulation affected aperiodic parameters:

$$
\text{Exponent} \sim 1 + S + (1 + S | \text{ROI}) + (1 + S | \text{subject})
$$

$$
\text{Offset} \sim 1 + S + (1 + S | \text{ROI}) + (1 + S | \text{subject})
$$

where $S$ represents stimulus condition (PRESTIM vs. STIM). We also fitted models for residual standard deviation (sigma) to capture heterogeneity in measurement precision across subjects and ROIs.

#### Main analysis: Exponent-ITPC relationship

For the primary analysis examining the exponent-ITPC relationship, we specified:

$$
\text{ITPC}_{\text{stim}} \sim 1 + \text{exponent}_z + (1 + \text{exponent}_z | \text{subject}) + (1 | \text{ROI})
$$

where $\text{exponent}_z$ represents the within-subject standardized spectral exponent (z-scored within each subject to remove between-subject baseline differences), and random effects account for both subject-specific variation in baseline ITPC and in the exponent-ITPC relationship, as well as ROI-specific baseline differences. This specification allows the exponent-ITPC relationship to vary across subjects while incorporating partial pooling across ROIs.

Z-normalization of the exponent facilitates interpretation, as the intercept represents expected ITPC when the exponent is at its subject-specific mean (exponent_z = 0). The slope coefficient represents the change in ITPC per 1 SD increase in spectral exponent.

We employed a Student's t-distribution likelihood (df = 3) to accommodate potential outliers. All models were fitted using 4 MCMC chains with 4,000 iterations each (1,000 warmup), with `adapt_delta` set to 0.95 to ensure adequate exploration of the posterior distribution.

#### Inference and multiple comparisons

For each ROI, we extracted posterior distributions for parameters of interest. We calculated posterior probabilities $P(\beta > 0 | \text{data})$ for positive effects and $P(\beta < 0 | \text{data})$ for negative effects.

To control for multiple comparisons across 148 cortical regions, RBA automatically adjusts inference thresholds through its modeling of the spatial structure. We considered effects credible when the posterior probability exceeded 0.95 (equivalent to a Bayesian analog of p < 0.05, two-tailed). Effect sizes were quantified as the predicted change in ITPC for a 1-SD increase in spectral exponent.

Convergence was assessed via $\hat{R} < 1.01$ for all parameters and visual inspection of trace plots. Model fit was evaluated using posterior predictive checks.

## Results

### Distribution of ITPC values

The distribution of ITPC values during pre-stimulus and stimulus periods is shown in @fig-dist-itpc. As expected, ITPC during the 40 Hz auditory stimulation (STIM condition) was substantially higher than during the pre-stimulus period (PRESTIM condition), confirming successful entrainment of neural oscillations to the external auditory rhythm.

![Distribution of ITPC values. Top: Pre-stimulus ITPC. Middle: Stimulus ITPC. Bottom: Change in ITPC (STIM - PRESTIM).](figures/chapter4/ch04-fig-dist-itpc.png){#fig-dist-itpc}

### Spatial distribution of ITPC

When all conditions were combined, the spatial pattern of ITPC revealed strong entrainment primarily in auditory cortices, with bilateral activation evident in superior temporal regions (@fig-brain-itpc). The difference between STIM and PRESTIM conditions showed that auditory stimulation induced robust phase-locking not only in primary auditory cortex but also in surrounding temporal, insular, and inferior sensorimotor regions.

![Spatial distribution of ITPC across cortical regions. Z-normalized values for PRE-SHAM and PRE-REAL conditions combined.](figures/chapter4/ch04-fig-brain-itpc.png){#fig-brain-itpc}

![ITPC difference effect (STIM - PRESTIM) showing regions with strongest auditory entrainment.](figures/chapter4/ch04-fig-brain-itpc-diff.png){#fig-brain-itpc-diff}

::: {.callout-note}
## Key findings from ITPC distribution
- Strong effect of auditory stimulus on ITPC in auditory regions, temporal lobe, inferior part of primary sensorimotor regions, and inferior frontal regions
- No regions showed evidence of different baseline ITPC between PRE-SHAM and PRE-REAL conditions (all P+ values between 0.10 and 0.90)
- No regions showed evidence of tDCS effects on ITPC (comparing POST vs. PRE or REAL vs. SHAM)
:::

### Distribution of aperiodic parameters

#### Spectral exponent

The distribution of spectral exponent values showed minimal differences between pre-stimulus and stimulus periods (@fig-dist-exponent), and no systematic changes due to auditory stimulation. This suggests that the aperiodic component of the power spectrum remains relatively stable during auditory entrainment, even as oscillatory power at 40 Hz increases substantially.

![Distribution of aperiodic exponent values and differences between conditions.](figures/chapter4/ch04-fig-dist-exponent.png){#fig-dist-exponent}

The spatial distribution of exponent values across cortical regions showed clear anatomical gradients, with steeper slopes (higher exponents) in frontal and temporal regions and flatter slopes in posterior and sensorimotor areas (@fig-brain-exponent).

![Z-normalized values of spectral exponent across cortical regions for PRE-SHAM and PRE-REAL conditions.](figures/chapter4/ch04-fig-brain-exponent.png){#fig-brain-exponent}

#### Spectral offset

The spectral offset showed similar stability across stimulus conditions (@fig-dist-offset), with no meaningful differences between pre-stimulus and stimulus periods. The spatial distribution of offset values was relatively uniform across cortical regions (@fig-brain-offset).

![Distribution of spectral offset values and differences between conditions.](figures/chapter4/ch04-fig-dist-offset.png){#fig-dist-offsett}

![Z-normalized offset values across cortical regions.](figures/chapter4/ch04-fig-brain-offset.png){#fig-brain-offset}

::: {.callout-note}
## Key findings from aperiodic parameters
- No evidence for effects of auditory stimulation on spectral exponent (Exponent ~ Stimulus)
- No evidence for effects of auditory stimulation on spectral offset
- No significant evidence for any models involving offset either as predicted variable or predictor
- These findings suggest that aperiodic parameters are relatively stable markers that are not substantially affected by transient auditory entrainment
:::

### Relationship between spectral exponent and ITPC

The primary analysis revealed a positive relationship between spectral exponent and ITPC during auditory stimulation across multiple brain regions. @fig-bsn2025 shows scatter plots for selected ROIs demonstrating this relationship, with data points colored by subject to illustrate both within-subject and between-subject consistency of the effect.

![Relationship between spectral exponent (z-scored) and ITPC across selected ROIs. Red lines indicate linear fits. Data points colored by subject show the consistency of the effect across individuals.](figures/chapter4/bsn2025.png){#fig-bsn2025}

The hierarchical Bayesian modeling revealed that higher spectral exponents (steeper 1/f slopes) were associated with stronger gamma synchrony (higher ITPC) during 40 Hz auditory entrainment. This positive relationship was particularly evident in auditory and temporal regions where ASSR responses were strongest.

::: {.callout-important}
## Main finding
Looking at the relationship between exponent and ITPC shows a positive association: higher exponent is associated with higher ITPC, indicating stronger synchrony during stimulation. This relationship was consistent across subjects and robust in regions showing strong auditory steady-state responses.
:::

The posterior distributions of coefficients estimated through hierarchical Bayesian modeling allowed us to assess both the magnitude and uncertainty of effects in each region. The multilevel structure enabled partial pooling of information across regions and subjects, providing more stable and interpretable estimates than traditional mass-univariate approaches.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Interpretation
The positive relationship between spectral exponent and ITPC suggests that steeper aperiodic slopes (reflecting greater dominance of inhibitory currents) are associated with stronger phase-locking to external rhythmic stimulation. This finding may seem counterintuitive if one expects greater inhibition to suppress oscillatory responses. However, it aligns with theoretical models suggesting that properly balanced inhibition is necessary for precise temporal coordination and phase-locking in gamma-generating circuits.
:::
